summary: NorthBridge is evaluating Redwood for regulated LLM workloads and wants a clear Hosted→Dedicated→Private path, with an emphasis on Private/VPC deployment. Key drivers are cost/latency predictability, isolation, and speeding up security review. The group agreed to schedule a Private/VPC technical deep dive with platform + security attendees and requested Redwood’s FinServ security FAQ language plus a reference architecture overview.

transcript:
NorthBridge Bank x Redwood Inference - Discovery (Private/VPC)
Recorded: 2026-01-09 14:03 ET (Fireflies)
Duration: 44 minutes

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood, AE)
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood, Solutions Engineering - Private/VPC)
- Maya Chen (NorthBridge, Director Platform Engineering)
- Raj Patel (NorthBridge, ML Eng Lead)
- Elena Garcia (NorthBridge, InfoSec/GRC)
- Tom Willis (NorthBridge, Procurement) (joined ~minute 31)

Auto-Summary (generated)
- NorthBridge is exploring a regulated inference platform that can run in a private network boundary (VPC) with clear retention controls and audit logs.
- Current solution is split between Bedrock for some workloads and limited external APIs for non-sensitive use cases; they are considering dedicated/self-host due to predictable cost/latency and compliance.
- Next step is a technical deep dive focused on Private/VPC architecture, logging/SIEM export, and key management (KMS/HSM).


[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. I think we’re recording. Maya, Raj, Elena, thanks for making time today. I’m Avery, I run point on our side. Colin is here as well, he’s our SE focused on the private deployments. 

[00:13] Maya Chen: Hey Avery. Yep, good to meet you. 

[00:16] Raj Patel: Hi.

[00:17] Elena Garcia: Hello.

[00:18] Colin O'Donnell: Hey everyone.

[00:20] Avery Johnson: Quick agenda: we’ll do like five minutes on what you’re trying to accomplish, current stack, constraints, and then we can talk about what Redwood can do, and mostly we’ll land on whether it makes sense to do a deeper technical session on Private/VPC. Sound okay?

[00:36] Maya Chen: Yep. That’s what we need.

[00:39] Avery Johnson: Great. Maybe Maya, do you want to kick us off with the business context? Like what triggered the evaluation.

[00:47] Maya Chen: Sure. So we’ve got a few internal teams building assistant-like things—agent assist for call center, and then some document understanding for internal policy and research. It started with just experimentation. Now we’re at the point where… security is like, okay, if this touches customer data, we need a real story.

[01:10] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[01:11] Maya Chen: And our platform group is trying to avoid every app team doing their own weird integration. So we want one inference layer we can standardize on.

[01:22] Avery Johnson: Got it. Raj, what are the actual workloads? Like chat, summarization, search.

[01:28] Raj Patel: Mostly summarization and extraction right now. Think: summarize a call transcript, extract entities, generate a follow-up email. We also have an internal knowledge base and we’re doing RAG. So embeddings, rerank, then generation.

[01:44] Raj Patel: Context sizes vary. Like the call center transcripts can be long. We try to chunk but still it’s not like tiny.

[01:52] Colin O'Donnell: When you say long, are we talking 8k tokens, 32k, 100k?

[01:58] Raj Patel: Today we aim for under 16k prompt tokens. But sometimes it spikes, especially if someone pastes a whole PDF. We want guardrails.

[02:08] Avery Johnson: And are these customer conversations, so that’s… regulated data?

[02:12] Elena Garcia: Yes. Customer PII, and in some cases financial info. Our compliance posture is GLBA and the FFIEC examiners are… not forgiving.

[02:24] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[02:25] Elena Garcia: We can do some de-identification, but we don’t want to depend on that as the only control.

[02:33] Avery Johnson: Totally. What’s your current inference setup? You mentioned experimentation.

[02:39] Raj Patel: We have two tracks. For low-risk internal stuff, we used OpenAI directly for a bit. That’s basically frozen now. 

[02:48] Raj Patel: For more “okay-ish” workloads, we use Bedrock. Mainly because we can keep it in our AWS account and there’s a story there.

[02:57] Maya Chen: But the challenge is we don’t get consistent performance and the cost predictability is hard. Also the model choices and quotas. When we do a load test it’s like, okay, this is fine, then it degrades.

[03:14] Colin O'Donnell: When it degrades, is it latency spikes or rate limiting or both?

[03:18] Maya Chen: Both. We’ve gotten throttled. And for some tasks we need streaming and it’s not always smooth.

[03:25] Avery Johnson: Okay. And is there any self-hosted today? Like vLLM or Triton.

[03:31] Raj Patel: We have a POC of vLLM on EKS with one of the smaller open models. It worked but we don’t want to run a mini GPU fleet ourselves as the default. 

[03:42] Raj Patel: Also KV cache—sorry if I say this wrong—KV cash, caching, it was complicated.

[03:49] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah KV cache. No worries.

[03:52] Avery Johnson: That’s basically why people come to us. So if I summarize, you want something production-grade but with deployment options.

[04:02] Elena Garcia: Deployment options and evidence. Like we need audit logs. We need to know exactly what data is stored, what isn’t, how long, who has access, encryption keys, etc.

[04:13] Avery Johnson: That’s helpful. Elena, can you share what “must haves” are for you in the first pass?

[04:20] Elena Garcia: Sure. I’ll be blunt. Data cannot be used for training. Prompts and outputs should not be retained by default—if there is retention it must be configurable and very short. We need access logs and admin actions logged. SSO/SAML. RBAC. 

[04:39] Elena Garcia: Encryption in transit, at rest, and ideally customer-managed keys. And ideally it’s in our VPC or at least private networking with no public endpoints.

[04:51] Colin O'Donnell: When you say customer-managed keys, do you mean AWS KMS in your account, or are you talking HSM, like CloudHSM?

[04:58] Elena Garcia: Long term it’s HSM. Short term, KMS is acceptable if it’s clearly separated. We also have key rotation requirements.

[05:09] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[05:10] Maya Chen: Also, we have data residency. US-only for these workloads, specifically us-east-1 preferred. 

[05:17] Avery Johnson: Okay.

[05:18] Raj Patel: And performance. Like, not just compliance. We need p95 latencies that are stable. Right now with Bedrock, it’s hard to give our product teams an SLO.

[05:29] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk about performance targets. Raj, what’s a good success metric? Like p95 under what for typical calls.

[05:37] Raj Patel: For our API tier, we’d love first token under 500 to 700 milliseconds for normal prompts. For longer summaries maybe it’s okay if it’s like 2 seconds, but it shouldn’t be 10.

[05:51] Raj Patel: Throughput wise, call center use case: we have peak times. Maybe 30 to 50 requests per second across the bank. But per team, smaller.

[06:03] Colin O'Donnell: And output tokens? 200, 1,000?

[06:06] Raj Patel: Typically 300 to 800. Sometimes 1500 for a long summary.

[06:13] Avery Johnson: Perfect, that gives us something. Also cost—do you have an internal target, like dollars per 1k tokens or monthly budget.

[06:22] Maya Chen: We’re still figuring it out. But we need predictability more than absolute cheapest. Like, we can’t have a surprise bill.

[06:32] Avery Johnson: Right, predictable unit economics.

[06:34] Elena Garcia: Also predictable controls. Like we don’t want “it depends” answers during security review.

[06:39] Avery Johnson: Totally fair.

[06:41] Colin O'Donnell: On deployment modes, have you decided you need private VPC day one? Or could you start with dedicated capacity that’s isolated but still managed by the vendor.

[06:52] Maya Chen: That’s what we’re debating. The platform team is leaning: start dedicated if it’s isolated enough, but security will ask about network path and whether it’s still public.

[07:03] Elena Garcia: For anything with customer PII, the preference is private networking. VPC endpoints, no public internet. If we can’t, then we need a compensating control story.

[07:14] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. Redwood has a “Hosted → Dedicated → Private” path. The Private option is in customer VPC with a private control plane / boundary. We should not go deep on architecture here, but that’s what the next session is for.

[07:28] Raj Patel: Okay.

[07:29] Maya Chen: Before we schedule, can you clarify what you mean by Private? Like is it you running in our AWS account? Or is it like an appliance.

[07:37] Colin O'Donnell: Good question. Private for us usually means we deploy the inference plane inside your VPC (and depending on arrangement, in your AWS account). Networking is private. You control routing and can integrate your KMS. Redwood still provides a control plane and updates, but we can design the boundaries. There’s also an on-prem package but that’s more specialized.

[08:02] Elena Garcia: Okay. And do you store prompts and outputs.

[08:07] Avery Johnson: Great question. By default, for regulated setups we don’t retain prompts/outputs for training, and retention is configurable. We can go through specifics and what’s logged for auditing. I want to be careful and align with our security docs so we’re consistent.

[08:23] Elena Garcia: Yeah I appreciate that. We will ask “where is it logged, where is it stored, for how long.”

[08:31] Colin O'Donnell: The audit logs we talk about are like access logs and admin action logs, and you can export to your SIEM. The content logs are separate. We can talk about what’s required for debugging vs privacy.

[08:44] Raj Patel: We also want prompt tracing for our engineers, but it can’t be wide open. Like only specific roles.

[08:52] Colin O'Donnell: That’s typical. Role-based access control and limiting who can view request content.

[08:59] Avery Johnson: Can I ask about internal stakeholders? Who needs to sign off. Elena obviously. Anyone else? Legal? Data privacy?

[09:06] Elena Garcia: Legal and privacy. Also vendor risk management. We have a standard questionnaire.

[09:14] Maya Chen: And procurement, though they come later.

[09:17] Avery Johnson: Great. Timeline wise, are you trying to do this in Q1?

[09:22] Maya Chen: Ideally yes. We have one product team that wants something in production by end of March, but I think that’s aggressive.

[09:31] Raj Patel: At least we want to pick a platform and get a POC running.

[09:35] Avery Johnson: Okay. We can usually do a scoped eval in a couple of weeks depending on security gates.

[09:42] Elena Garcia: Security gates is the thing. If we can get evidence quickly, it helps.

[09:47] Avery Johnson: That’s actually part of why we’re doing a regulated workload motion this quarter—having pre-approved FAQ language and reference architecture to speed up reviews.

[09:58] Maya Chen: Good.

[10:00] Colin O'Donnell: Raj, model preferences? Are you locked into Bedrock models? Or are you open to open-source models if quality is okay.

[10:09] Raj Patel: Open. We do evals. Our issue is less “must be X model” and more “quality and reliability.” But we do have some teams that want Claude via Bedrock. 

[10:21] Raj Patel: We also looked at Azure OpenAI because the bank already has some Microsoft contracts.

[10:27] Avery Johnson: Yep. We run and optimize a curated set of models and we can discuss what fits your tasks. And we do offer routing and fallback between compatible variants if capacity is constrained.

[10:40] Maya Chen: The fallback is interesting. We had incidents where an endpoint just got slow and the app team had no plan B.

[10:47] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. You can define policies: latency threshold then failover, or region failover, or model variant fallback. Again, details in the deep dive.

[10:58] Elena Garcia: As long as failover doesn’t violate residency.

[11:01] Colin O'Donnell: Right. Residency constraints are part of routing policy.

[11:05] Avery Johnson: Can you share any “red lines” so we don’t waste time? Like must be on-prem.

[11:12] Maya Chen: On-prem is not a requirement right now. Some teams asked, but we’re AWS-first for this.

[11:20] Elena Garcia: The red line is public internet exposure for customer data. And unclear retention.

[11:27] Avery Johnson: Very clear.

[11:29] Raj Patel: And for ML team, we need to see consistent performance on our prompts. We’ll want to run a small eval set.

[11:36] Avery Johnson: Yes, that’s normal.

[11:38] Colin O'Donnell: If you can share a redacted prompt set, we can run it in a benchmark environment and show latency/cost. Or we can do it in your environment during the POC.

[11:50] Raj Patel: We can share redacted patterns, yes.

[11:54] Avery Johnson: Elena, what’s the usual NDA process? Are you comfortable reviewing some evidence under NDA.

[12:01] Elena Garcia: We generally require NDA before sharing certain items, but we can start with high-level docs without. Once it gets to SOC reports and things, NDA.

[12:12] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[12:13] Colin O'Donnell: On the technical side, for Private/VPC, common questions are VPC peering vs PrivateLink, DNS, TLS termination, egress allow lists, and where logs go. For the deep dive we’ll want your network person or at least someone who knows the constraints.

[12:30] Maya Chen: I can bring someone from network. But I can answer basics.

[12:33] Avery Johnson: Great.

[12:35] Colin O'Donnell: Also, do you have a SIEM standard? Splunk, Sentinel?

[12:39] Elena Garcia: Splunk for most logs. Some teams use Sentinel but Splunk is primary.

[12:46] Colin O'Donnell: Okay, so we should talk export formats. Usually it’s like JSON over HTTPS to an endpoint, or pushing to your logging pipeline.

[12:56] Raj Patel: And do you support OpenTelemetry.

[12:59] Colin O'Donnell: We have tracing hooks, yes. We can discuss what’s available GA vs limited.

[13:06] Avery Johnson: We’ll keep it honest—no overpromising.

[13:10] Maya Chen: Appreciate.

[13:12] Avery Johnson: Let me pause—any other drivers? Why not just standardize on Bedrock and call it a day.

[13:20] Raj Patel: Performance consistency is one. Also model ops. We want to be able to pin versions, do canaries, measure regressions. Bedrock is kind of a black box.

[13:33] Maya Chen: And we want predictable capacity. We had a case where we asked for quota, it took a while.

[13:41] Avery Johnson: Yep. That’s what Dedicated is for, and Private too.

[13:45] Elena Garcia: Another driver is audit. Bedrock gives some cloud trail style logs, but it’s still fuzzy for our app teams. They want per-route auditability.

[13:54] Colin O'Donnell: We can do per-route and per-model logs and tie to API keys or identities. And you can integrate with SSO for the console.

[14:05] Avery Johnson: Speaking of console, do you want your engineers to see token-level cost metrics.

[14:10] Raj Patel: Yes. That would be huge. Right now we estimate. 

[14:15] Raj Patel: We also care about batching and caching but we don’t want to rebuild that ourselves.

[14:22] Colin O'Donnell: That’s part of our runtime—continuous batching, prefix caching. Sometimes people say “KV cash” and it is cash in a way. 

[14:31] Raj Patel: (laughs) Yeah.

[14:33] Avery Johnson: Okay. So I think we have enough to justify next step.

[14:38] Avery Johnson: Before we get there, can we clarify: do you need a vendor that will sign specific SLAs.

[14:45] Maya Chen: Eventually. For POC, not necessarily. But for production yes.

[14:50] Elena Garcia: And we’ll need DPA language. And we may ask about BCP/DR.

[14:58] Avery Johnson: Yep. We can provide standard terms and we can talk about uptime commitments in Dedicated/Private.

[15:05] Colin O'Donnell: For DR, we can do multi-AZ and regional options, but again subject to residency.

[15:12] Elena Garcia: Right.

[15:13] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk about what the technical deep dive should cover so it’s useful. Maya, Raj, Elena—what do you want to walk away with.

[15:24] Maya Chen: I want a clear architecture: what runs where, what network connectivity, what endpoints are public or private.

[15:31] Raj Patel: I want to know how we’d run an eval, and what knobs we have for latency vs cost.

[15:36] Elena Garcia: I want crisp answers on: do you store prompts/outputs, how are they encrypted, what audit logs exist, and how we can export them. And what evidence you provide, like SOC 2.

[15:49] Avery Johnson: Great. We can do that.

[15:51] Colin O'Donnell: We also should align on shared responsibility: what Redwood manages vs what your team manages in Private.

[15:58] Maya Chen: Yes.

[16:00] Avery Johnson: Cool. I’ll propose times for next week. Before we end, any other questions.

[16:07] Raj Patel: Minor question—do you support both embeddings and chat in the same environment.

[16:12] Avery Johnson: Yes, same API surface. 

[16:14] Colin O'Donnell: In Private, it depends on which models you install, but yes, the platform supports it.

[16:20] Elena Garcia: When you say “install”, is it like Kubernetes.

[16:25] Colin O'Donnell: It can run on Kubernetes in the VPC. There’s an installer and we help with it. Again, we’ll show the reference architecture.

[16:34] Maya Chen: Okay.

[16:35] Avery Johnson: I’ll send a recap email with next steps. Also, we have a FinServ security FAQ addendum with approved language on retention, residency, audit logs, KMS options. I’ll include that. 

[16:49] Elena Garcia: Good. That will help.

[16:52] Avery Johnson: Raj, if you can send even just rough estimates of RPS, prompt length distributions, we can come prepared.

[17:00] Raj Patel: Yep. We can do that.

[17:02] Colin O'Donnell: And if you have preference on connectivity: PrivateLink vs peering. Some banks prefer PrivateLink.

[17:08] Maya Chen: We usually prefer PrivateLink. Peering is possible but there’s more approvals.

[17:14] Colin O'Donnell: That’s helpful.

[17:16] Avery Johnson: Elena, anything else we should avoid—like marketing claims that annoy you.

[17:21] Elena Garcia: Just don’t say “HIPAA” (laughs). We’re a bank. But seriously, don’t say “we’re compliant with everything.” We need specifics.

[17:30] Avery Johnson: Totally. We’ll keep it specific.

[17:34] (crosstalk)

[17:35] Maya Chen: Also, we’ll probably want our vendor risk person on the next call.

[17:39] Avery Johnson: Great, invite them.

[17:41] Colin O'Donnell: And network/security engineering if possible.

[17:44] Avery Johnson: Okay. Thanks all. I’ll send follow-up today with times and docs.

[17:52] Elena Garcia: Thanks.

[17:53] Raj Patel: Thanks.

[17:54] Maya Chen: Thank you.

[17:56] Avery Johnson: Alright, talk soon.
